 Why This Matters 
 ACA premiums are rising again. What does that mean for consumers?
 Lara Salahi and Joseph Burns 
 November 9, 2026 
 Share:
 Photo by Tima Miroshnichenko via pexels
 Americans buying health insurance through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace are facing another round of premium increases. Benchmark silver premiums are expected to rise an average of 13% in 2027, following an even steeper 26% increase in 2026, according to a new analysis from KFF .
 The increases come as open enrollment starts for 2027 coverage, forcing consumers to weigh whether to keep their current plans, switch to less expensive coverage or forgo insurance altogether.
 For health journalists, double-digit premium increases offer a chance to link national health policy changes to every family’s finances. Reporters can also explain the differences between states running their own ACA marketplaces (also called Obamacare) and those that rely on the federal marketplace, as KFF explained. 
 In the 27 states using the federal Healthcare.gov system, the benchmark silver premiums are rising 11%, five percentage points lower than in states that run their own enrollment systems, where premiums are rising 16%, KFF noted.
 Rising costs threaten coverage and access to care 
 Paying more for Affordable Care Act coverage is just one of many ways consumers are struggling financially, according to two recent Commonwealth Fund reports.
 First, the number of uninsured Americans will rise to 37 million by 2036 — about the same as in 2014, when most of the Affordable Care Act’s changes took effect, the fund reported on Oct. 22. That report, “ The State of Health Insurance Coverage in 2026 ,” showed almost half (46%) of adults ages 19-64 have inadequate health insurance, 12% have had a gap in coverage, 23% have been underinsured and 11% uninsured. Being underinsured means coverage did not provide affordable access to care. The report also found that more people (50%) delayed or avoided care because of cost than in 2022.
 Second, fast-rising health costs increase levels of medical debt, the fund explained in a Sept. 17 report, “ How Medical Bills and Debt Impact Americans with Private Insurance .” Other costs beyond rising premium rates make care unaffordable. “High out-of-pocket costs and plan deductibles can make health care difficult to afford,” the fund showed. Recent federal policies have exacerbated these problems, as Reed Abelson reported for The New York Times earlier this year.
 In the insurance coverage report, the Commonwealth Fund showed that from 2010 through 2025, the proportion of uninsured Americans fell from nearly 16% to 8%, mostly due to the ACA’s coverage expansions and enhanced premium tax credits. But in 2025, the Trump administration and Congress enacted legislation that cut federal funding for Medicaid and made changes to the Affordable Care Act marketplaces, the report explained.
 “The country is on the brink of undoing years of progress in health coverage,” the report’s authors noted. “Stripping insurance from millions of people will deepen an affordability crisis that already leaves too many going without care or paying off medical debt. Congress can prevent more people from losing coverage by restoring enhanced marketplace premium tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts. Without that action, millions of families will face the cost of getting sick with no insurance at all.”
 Why premiums are increasing 
 Several factors are contributing to higher health insurance costs. When Congress failed to extend the enhanced premium tax credit subsidies in December 2025, coverage became more expensive for many enrollees in Affordable Care Act plans. Introduced during COVID-19, the financial assistance lowered monthly premiums and led to record enrollment over four years (2022 through 2025), including 24.3 million last year. 
 Ending the enhanced subsidies forced consumers to pay much more for the same coverage. People with incomes above 400% of the federal poverty level  generally no longer qualify for a subsidy, while others may receive less assistance.
 Insurers also point to rising health care costs, including hospital prices, prescription drug spending and increased use of medical services, as reasons for raising premiums.
 The higher costs are already affecting enrollment. KFF reported Oct. 14 that the number of individuals enrolled in Affordable Care Act marketplaces fell by more than 4.6 million people, from 25.2 million in June 2025 to 20.5 million in June 2026. 
 Such a drop can cause insurers to raise rates because when relatively healthy people drop coverage, insurers may be left with a smaller pool of people with greater health care needs.
 Some consumers also are choosing less expensive plans with higher deductibles, which can lower their monthly premiums. But high deductibles make them responsible for thousands of dollars in out-of-pocket costs before insurance covers services. Also, the Commonwealth Fund showed that rising out-of-pocket costs can lead to medical debt.
 Reporting angles to explore 
 National averages can obscure significant differences among states, counties and income groups. Here are several questions worth pursuing locally:
 Who pays the most? Talk to self-employed people, small-business owners, farmers and early retirees who depend on individual-market coverage. Before they turn 65 and become eligible for Medicare, older adults can face particularly steep premiums. Ask whether those consumers will drop their coverage as their monthly costs rise.
 Are people leaving the ACA marketplaces? Compare state enrollment figures from 2025 and 2026. Are consumers dropping insurance altogether, switching to less expensive plans or moving to plans with higher deductibles?
 Are fewer insurance choices available? Find out whether insurers are entering or leaving the state’s marketplace. Are people losing access to particular plans, hospitals, physicians or provider networks?
 Who is getting financial assistance? Not everyone will experience the same premium increase. Some lower-income consumers will continue receiving subsidies that offset much of the costs. Explain the difference between an insurance plan’s full monthly premium and what an individual actually pays after financial assistance.
 Are people delaying care because of higher costs? Interview consumers who have moved to plans with higher deductibles. Are they postponing appointments, skipping prescriptions or avoiding recommended tests because they cannot afford the out-of-pocket expenses?
 Where to find data 
 A few resources can help reporters put together a local picture:
 KFF has extensive resources on Affordable Care Act enrollment, premium costs, subsidy changes and state-by-state comparisons.
 CMS and HealthCare.gov provide federal enrollment information, plan availability and policy updates.
 State insurance departments track insurers’ rate filings, approve or reject premium-increase requests, and explain what drives up costs.
 State-based marketplace websites have county-level plan comparisons, benchmark premiums and enrollment information.
 State Medicaid agencies report on the number of people who may be losing coverage or becoming eligible for other public programs.
 Questions to ask 
 Consumers are an important part of this story, but so are the people helping them navigate their options. Talk to insurance brokers, state insurance regulators, hospital representatives and health policy researchers.
 Ask consumers not just how much their premiums have increased, but whether they can still afford their coverage, what they’ve had to give up to maintain it, and whether they expect to remain insured in 2027.
 A bigger question is what happens when health insurance becomes too expensive for the people who need it. Following consumers through open enrollment into the new year can help journalists document the consequences of rising costs and changing federal policy — from coverage losses to delayed care and rising financial strain on families.
